source.title: How Optimality Structures Sparse Dictionaries: A Theory for Understanding SAE Representations

page_placements.theme: SAE objectives admit low-loss solutions that differ from the true features (theory and toy)

record.tranche_reason: The study derives theoretical constraints that explain hierarchical splitting and absorption as consequences of dictionary-learning optimality, and argues that widening dictionaries refines their categories. It also qualifies the feature-hierarchy interpretation rather than simply reproducing a size-scaling experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper gives theoretical results about splitting, absorption, and width, but does not directly match features across SAE dictionary sizes or measure whether split features cover the same inputs and have nearby directions. Its empirical SAE experiments test optimality conditions on training and shifted data, not feature splitting itself. The cited examples and results from other studies are not recorded as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: A theoretical argument, with toy simulations, that hierarchical splitting and absorption are optima imposed by the L1 dictionary-learning objective. It also argues that widening keeps splitting until each data ray from the optimal bias has its own atom. These bear on V1, V4, V5 and V6. No SAE size sweep matches features across widths, and the GPT2-small experiments test optimality conditions, not splitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that dictionary-learning optimality alone structures SAE representations. They argue it explains hierarchical splitting and absorption (absorption being splitting with a 'none of the others' category), residual structure, dense antipodal pairs and unbounded splitting with width. They present the conditions as a diagnostic that real SAEs pass in-distribution and fail off-distribution. They caution that the conditions are necessary, not sufficient, cover vanilla dictionary learning only, and are tested pairwise on feature subsets.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives results for idealized vanilla dictionary learning with latent codes optimized directly, rather than directly comparing trained SAE feature matches across dictionary sizes. It also tests released SAEs against theoretical optimality conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimality-condition violations increase with distance from the training layer or dataset; some layer and dataset shifts show no violations while others do.

fits_no_version.finding: A 24,576-latent GPT2-small layer-8 SAE shows no pairwise optimality violations on OWT. Applied to other layers or datasets, violations appear (0–146 pairs) and are all strict hierarchies not present in the training data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary-learning optimality conditions hold for SAEs on their training distribution and fail, as spurious strict hierarchies, under distribution or layer shift.

record.problems: The authors state that their conditions are necessary rather than sufficient, are derived for vanilla dictionary learning rather than specific encoders, and are tested only pairwise and on feature subsets. The main feature-splitting conclusions are theoretical; the experiments do not directly compare matched features across dictionary sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports dataset-shift pairwise and joint-condition tests and residual-condition tests across datasets and widths in Appendix D. These were left out because they test optimality diagnostics rather than the feature-splitting, absorption, or cross-size matching behavior named by the claim.

untested.parts: No trained SAE size sweep. No measurement that finer features cover the coarse feature's inputs or lie near its direction.
Whole version. GPT2-small SAEs are used only for optimality-condition tests.
Whole version. No cross-size family geometry and no comparison with the model's own concept hierarchy.
Whether changing SAE size or sparsity removes absorption.
Decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents; novel latents across sizes.

missing.what: Toy wide-dictionary simulations: a 30-neuron dictionary on 2D cross data uses only 4 active neurons; a 10-neuron scalar encoding uses 2. Further width yields no further splitting beyond the ray count.
missing.locator: Section 7, Fig 5D; Appendix E.5, Fig 6; Fig 4C

missing.what: Toy two-element dictionary training showing features are stable only where the convex-hull condition holds (amodularity index vs cosine).

record.verdict_notes: All version-relevant results are theoretical or from toy simulations; no trained-SAE size comparison. Verdicts rest on derivations, so they establish mechanism and plausibility rather than empirical rates. The study cites, rather than being, any of the original sources. The feature-splitting SAE family (768–6,144 latents) is used only for the residual-condition test.

versions.untested_parts: No direct feature matching across increasing SAE sizes; no measurement that split features cover roughly the same inputs or lie near the original direction.
No test of the splitting pattern across large models or broadly across open SAE releases.
No empirical measurement of whether split features' directions are geometrically close.
No empirical comparison of SAE sizes or sparsity levels to test whether they remove absorption.
No direct decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, nor measurement of novel latents across sizes.
No comparison with Matryoshka SAEs or other objectives; the splitting argument is theoretical rather than a controlled objective comparison.

rows.subject: vanilla dictionary learning (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives a necessary feature-direction and activity-distribution condition for local optimality.

conditions.value: hierarchical features; lower-level feature activates only when higher-level feature is active

rows.measure: whether the hierarchical parent and child can both occur in an optimal representation
rows.value: Unless their dictionary directions are perfectly aligned, the hierarchical features are unstable and will not both appear in an optimal representation.
rows.note: The result rules against coexistence of a nested parent-child family except in the perfect-alignment case; it does not measure the directions of features produced by an SAE size sweep.
rows.check: Linked to V3 in the record. The result concerns whether a parent and child can coexist within one optimal dictionary, not whether families across sizes are nested or geometrically close, so V3 is dropped. It bears on V4 (the parent cannot stably fire with its child) and on V6 (the instability comes from the objective). Theoretical derivation, not a measurement.

rows.subject: vanilla dictionary learning (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Uses the local-optimality condition to explain hierarchical feature splitting.

conditions.value: nonnegative sparse dictionary learning with L1 penalty

rows.measure: stability of a representation that separates lower-level categories
rows.value: Splitting a hierarchy into mutually exclusive lower-level categories makes the features stable under the condition derived in the paper.
rows.note: This is a theoretical explanation of splitting as a consequence of the dictionary-learning objective, not a direct comparison of trained dictionaries at different sizes.
rows.check: Linked to V1 in the record. The row shows that mutually exclusive lower-level categories are the stable optimum, but it does not involve dictionary size, so V1 is dropped. Theoretical.

rows.subject: vanilla dictionary learning (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Applies the feature optimality condition to feature absorption.

conditions.value: hierarchical features with overlapping high- and low-level features

rows.measure: whether a higher-level feature can remain optimal when it co-activates hierarchically with a lower-level feature
rows.value: Absorbing instances of co-activity into the lower-level feature can turn the representation into mutually exclusive categories and stabilize it.
rows.note: The paper presents absorption as a route to stability analogous to splitting.
rows.check: Absorption is derived as a stabilising optimum of the objective, which also bears on V6. The claim that changing size or sparsity doesn't fix it is not tested.

rows.subject: vanilla dictionary learning (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the globally optimal representation in the wide-dictionary limit.

conditions.value: datapoints grouped by rays from the optimal bias

rows.measure: structure and minimum width of a global optimum
rows.value: A one-dictionary-atom-per-datapoint solution is globally optimal; the narrowest global optimum is governed by the number of rays from the optimal bias needed to reach datapoints farther than λ from it.
rows.note: This supports width-dependent refinement in the theoretical setting, but does not establish same-input coverage or nearby directions for features across widths.
rows.check: The wide-limit result predicts splitting continues with width up to one atom per data ray, which bears on V1. It also bears on V5's 'no size gives a complete set'. However, it implies a narrowest global optimum set by the ray count, so V5 holds only partly. Does not show input coverage or nearby directions.

relation.reason: Derives its own results on splitting, absorption and wide-limit behaviour.

tranche.reason: Theory argues that splitting and absorption are optima of the objective (V6) and derives wide-limit splitting behaviour bearing on V1, V4 and V5. No SAE size sweep.

source_check.notes: Theory paper, plus GPT2-small layer-8 SAE diagnostics. The conditions are necessary, not sufficient, and tested only pairwise and on subsets. Wide limit: one-atom-per-datapoint and one-atom-per-ray solutions are equally optimal. The per-ray solution is the narrowest and is stable to new neurons. 'Cap' and 'terminal width' readings mean no loss gain from extra width; they do not mean further splitting is impossible.

statements.correction: Sec 7/App F: the narrowest global optimum has one atom per ray from b (minus a λ-ball); new neurons cannot lower the loss (eq. 10); one-atom-per-datapoint is also a global optimum. Fig 5D: 30-neuron dictionary on 2D cross, 4 active. Fig 6/App E.5: 10 neurons, 2 active; the optimiser 'somehow' picks this among degenerate optima.
statements.problem: The 4-of-30 and 2-of-10 toy results are right. 'Caps splitting in theory' overstates: in theory, one atom per ray is only the narrowest global optimum. Wider solutions, such as one atom per datapoint, are equally optimal.
Does not mention this study; nothing about it to check.
Only classifies this study as theory, which is correct.

statements.correction: Layer-8 SAE (24,576 latents) on OWT: 0 pairwise violations (3,700 features, 14M pairs). Layers 4, 6, 7, 9, 10: 146, 22, 0, 0, 3 violating pairs, all strict hierarchies (App D.3). Datasets: English Wikipedia 0; French/German Wikipedia and code have violations that 'tend to be hierarchical'. The hierarchies are not present on OWT (App D.5).
statements.problem: The 0-146 range covers layer shift only; per-dataset violation counts are figure-only. The text calls only the layer-shift violations 'all strict hierarchies'. For dataset shift it says they 'tend to be hierarchical'.
